title: Fiasco’s production of The Verge by Susan Glaspell at The Public Thea...
transcript: A romantically elusive botanist teeters between creation and destruction. “Are we in Bushwick?” you may ask. Actually, it's 1921 in some unspecified greenhouse where Claire Archer, suffocated by the pressures of domesticity, is plunging herself into the creation of new plant species. As a coproduction between The Public and Fiasco, which is widely known for its ensemble work, I find this play a strange choice, as it feels more like a character study where Claire is saddled with almost half the script. She is a peculiar character, one who is undoubtedly working against the grain as a headstrong 1920s woman resistant to motherhood, complacency and traditional gender roles. Everyone around her, which is mostly men, is completely baffled by her, despite her vigorous attempts to convey her philosophies around life and how she wants hers to be. I found her to be too sprawling in her ideas to adequately characterize her, causing her opacity to overshadow the ideas she expresses. Although you could argue that the play is meant to critique precisely this dynamic where a woman is seen as too complex for everyone else to understand, we the audience need sufficient insight into her so that we can invest in her as a protagonist, or at least an antihero. Act 1 opens a wide series of philosophical threads that aren't really grounded in meaningful backstory with respect to Claire, nor are they picked up on in Act 2. This leaves the ideas to fend for themselves — I can see them being ahead of their time in 1921, but they feel dated in 2026, even in an elegantly staged production such as this one.
